metadata.title: The development of student teachers’ teacher self-efficacy before and during the COVID-19 pandemic

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study uses a longitudinal quasi-experimental design with student-teacher participants from a single large German university in Brandenburg, collected at three waves (T1, T2, T3) during semester weeks 1, 9, and 13. The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and the analysis is based on latent growth curve modeling rather than ILSA-style population inference. Because no sampling frame or weight variables are described, the results should be interpreted as pertaining to the analytic sample rather than as nationally representative estimates. For any future re-use with survey-weighted inference, analysts would need to identify whether any sampling weights exist in the original project dataset; none are documented here.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are teacher self-efficacy scale scores measured via Likert-type items (Instructional Strategies, Classroom Management, Student Engagement) and modeled with latent growth curve models; the paper does not use cognitive achievement plausible values (PVs). Missing-data handling is not specified as an imputation/deletion strategy for the analytic models; instead, the authors report a Little’s MCAR test and describe inclusion based on having data for at least two of three waves, but they do not document a formal missing-data procedure for remaining missingness. This is therefore a reporting gap for missing-data treatment in the longitudinal modeling context.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were student teachers at a large German university in Brandenburg. The analytic sample (N=201) was drawn from a larger longitudinal project (N=352) and included only those who (a) had teacher self-efficacy data for at least two of the three waves (T1, T2, T3) and (b) were taught either exclusively face-to-face (summer 2019 and winter 2019/20 combined; n=80) or entirely online during the first COVID-19 lockdown (summer 2020; n=121). The authors report running Little’s MCAR test to assess whether missingness was completely at random, and they note that included participants differed from excluded ones on initial self-efficacy and prior pedagogical experience.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (not used); student-teacher longitudinal self-efficacy (Germany, Brandenburg; T1-T3 across one semester)
main_findings.target_variable: Self-efficacy for instructional strategies (latent growth slope / AGF)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Latent growth curve model fit: face-to-face c2(1)=1.37, p=.24, CFI=0.924, RMSEA=0.068, SRMR=0.086; COVID-19 c2(3)=4.12, p=.24, CFI=0.991, RMSEA=0.056, SRMR=0.178. Additional growth factor (AGF) mean: M=-0.01, p<.05. Interaction (intercept × AGF): b=0.03, p=.06 (non-significant). Additional analysis (Self-efficacy for classroom management (latent growth slope / AGF)): Latent growth curve model fit: face-to-face c2(1)=0.56, p=.46, CFI=1.000, RMSEA=0.000, SRMR=0.033; COVID-19 c2(1)=0.14, p=.70, CFI=1.000, RMSEA=0.000, SRMR=0.007. Slope means: face-to-face M=0.02, p<.01; COVID-19 M=0.00, p=.27. Multi-group with AGF: c2(5)=9.52, p=.09, CFI=0.970, RMSEA=0.095, SRMR=0.322; AGF mean M=-0.01, p<.05. Interaction (intercept × AGF): b=0.04, p<.01; with covariates, interaction became non-significant (b=0.02, p=.26). Additional analysis (Self-efficacy for student engagement (latent growth slope / AGF)): Latent growth curve model fit: face-to-face c2(1)=0.75, p=.39, CFI=1.000, RMSEA=0.000, SRMR=0.030; COVID-19 c2(1)=0.01, p=.93, CFI=1.000, RMSEA=0.000, SRMR=0.001. Slope means: face-to-face M=0.02, p<.01; COVID-19 M=-0.01, p<.05. Multi-group with AGF: c2(5)=9.60, p=.09, CFI=0.973, RMSEA=0.096, SRMR=0.265; AGF mean M=-0.02, p<.01. Interaction (intercept × AGF): b=0.03, p<.05; with covariates, gender moderated the intercept–AGF (b=-0.02, p<.05) and prior pedagogical experience moderated (b=0.01, p<.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using student-teacher longitudinal self-efficacy data from Germany (Brandenburg) across one semester (T1–T3), the study leveraged COVID-19 vs face-to-face group membership (with gender and prior pedagogical experience tested as moderators) to model self-efficacy for instructional strategies, finding that the COVID-19 group showed significantly less change across time than the face-to-face group (AGF mean negative and significant), while the intercept–AGF interaction was small and non-significant. This indicates that disruptions to practical experiences during COVID-19 may have reduced developmental gains in instructional-strategy self-efficacy, though the overall within-group change was largely stagnant and moderation effects were limited.

data.outcome_summary: This paper analyzes longitudinal change in student teachers’ teacher self-efficacy across three waves (T1, T2, T3) during a single semester in Germany (Brandenburg). The analytic sample comprised N=201 student teachers from one university, split into a face-to-face group (n=80; summer 2019 and winter 2019/20 combined) and a COVID-19 group (n=121; summer 2020 taught entirely online). Using latent growth curve models with an additional growth factor, the authors found that self-efficacy for instructional strategies showed little within-group change but significantly less developmental change in the COVID-19 group relative to face-to-face. For classroom management, self-efficacy increased in the face-to-face group but stayed constant in the COVID-19 group (AGF mean negative and significant). For student engagement, self-efficacy increased face-to-face but declined under COVID-19 (AGF mean negative and significant), with moderation effects involving gender and prior pedagogical experience. Limitations include unequal group sizes and incomplete documentation of missing-data handling beyond inclusion criteria.
